sections.label: Committee completes unanimous report
sections.summary: The Committee, with Government and Opposition MPs, completed deliberations and unanimously agreed on a report.

sentences.speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
sentences.text: The Committee, comprising both Government and Opposition Members of Parliament, has completed its deliberations and unanimously agreed on a report.

sections.label: Parliament informed of President's inaction
sections.summary: The first recommendation is for Parliament to be kept informed if the President fails to exercise custodial powers within constitutional time limits.

sentences.speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
sentences.text: The first recommendation is for Parliament to be kept informed if the President fails to exercise his custodial powers on a measure passed by Parliament within the time limits prescribed by the Constitution.

sections.label: Parliament overruling presidential veto
sections.summary: The second recommendation concerns Parliament's power to overrule the President if he vetoes contrary to the CPA's recommendation.

sentences.speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
sentences.text: The second recommendation concerns Parliament's power to overrule the President if he exercises a veto contrary to the recommendation of the Council of Presidential Advisers (CPA).

sections.label: Notice of amendments increased
sections.summary: Notice of amendments should be increased from two clear days to four clear days.

sentences.speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
sentences.text: First, notice of amendments should be increased from two clear days to four clear days.

sections.label: Tracked amendments for amendment Bills
sections.summary: For amendment Bills, AGC law drafters will start a July project to make tracked amendments against the main Act available.

sentences.speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
sentences.text: For amendment Bills, I would like to inform the House that the law drafters at AGC will commence on a project in July to make available tracked amendments against the main Act.

sections.label: Ad hoc increase in Question Time
sections.summary: The Government will ask the House to increase Question Time on an ad hoc basis if the volume of business permits.

sentences.speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
sentences.text: What the Government will do is to ask the House to increase Question Time on an ad hoc basis if the volume of business permits.

sections.label: Average sitting hours per Parliament
sections.summary: The 11th Parliament averaged five hours eight minutes per Sitting day, while this Parliament averaged six hours 23 minutes up to April.

sentences.speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
sentences.text: For the 11th Parliament, we sat for an average of five hours and eight minutes per Sitting day.

sentences.speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
sentences.text: The average for this Parliament, up to April, is six hours and 23 minutes.

sections.label: Deleting Standing Order 54(4)
sections.summary: The passage discusses the spirit of the Standing Order and how deleting Standing Order 54(4) could allow a Motion to pass with 17 ayes and 9 nos.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: It would appear that the spirit of this Standing Order is not just to ensure no infringement of the rights of the minority or an abuse of the rules of Parliament, but to ensure that there is a significant enough number of Members of Parliament who are present in the House to see through any debate and at the close of debate.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: However, what these amendments could considerably do is to create a public impression that the deletion of Standing Order No 54(4) supports the presence of fewer Members of Parliament in the House when the relevant question is put, bearing in mind that the deleted Standing Order does not call for a quorum of 25 Members but the presence of at least 25 Members who were in support of the Motion, a higher requirement necessitating a sufficiently robust number of Members of Parliament in the House.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: So, for example, if these amendments are approved and Standing Order 54(4) is deleted, it would permit a hypothetical Motion to pass should the matter be decided with 17 "ayes" and 9 "nos", as it would have met the constitutional quorum requirement of at least 26 Members.

sections.label: Support for amendments and question priority
sections.summary: The Member supports the amendments but asks the Leader whether certain questions will be given priority, citing repeatedly postponed questions last year.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The registration of my concerns notwithstanding, I support the amendments.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Can I get some understanding from the Leader as to whether those questions will be accorded some degree of priority in the subsequent session of Parliament, because my experience in the second half of last year was that a question on the Competition of Commissioner of Singapore and lifts, with regard to lifts that are maintained by or managed by EM Services, was repeatedly postponed month after month.

sections.label: Amending Standing Order 18 for petitions
sections.summary: The Standing Orders Committee proposes amending Standing Order 18 to let the House decide that a petition need not be referred to the Public Petitions Committee.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The proposal by the Standing Orders Committee is to amend Standing Order 18 to provide an option for the House to decide that a petition need not be referred to the Public Petitions Committee (PPC).

sections.label: Concern over petitions not heard
sections.summary: The Member is concerned that routine use of the new power would mean petitions are not given due hearing or signal that petitions are unimportant.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The Standing Order provides that every such petition must be referred to the PPC, except in very limited circumstances.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: I am concerned that this new power, if used routinely, would result in petitions not being given their due hearing, or send a signal that petitions are not important.

sections.label: Public Petitions Committee powers
sections.summary: The PPC can call for witnesses, papers and records and can independently report its opinion and observations to Parliament.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: PPC is empowered to call for witnesses, papers and records and can independently report its opinion and its observations to Parliament.

sections.label: Judicious use of Standing Order 18
sections.summary: The new power under Standing Order 18 should be used most judiciously, given the importance of the public petitions process.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: In summary, Madam, while the new power under Standing Order 18 is a useful power to have, my view is that it should be used most judiciously, bearing in mind the importance of the public petitions process.

sections.label: Proposals on veto and Bill procedures
sections.summary: Proposals cover Parliament overriding a presidential veto and longer notice periods for Bills and amendments.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
sentences.text: One of the proposals states that if the President goes against the advice of the majority of the Council of Presidential Advisers, and exercises his veto power, Parliament can override such a veto with a two-thirds majority.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
sentences.text: For this to happen, the President's grounds and Council's recommendation should be made available at least two days before a Motion is moved to overrule the President.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
sentences.text: Second, on the Bill procedures, I welcome the proposal to increase the minimum interval from seven to 10 clear days as this will give more time for further deliberation on Bills.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
sentences.text: I also welcome the increase in the notice period for amendments from two clear days to four clear days as this will strike an appropriate balance between passing legislation in a timely way, while allowing Parliament adequate time for legislative scrutiny.

sections.label: Amendments passed and EP issues
sections.summary: The amendments were passed and came into force last month, leaving two narrow procedural issues for the EP.

sentences.speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
sentences.text: The amendments were passed by Parliament and came into force last month.

sentences.speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
sentences.text: So far as the EP is concerned, there are only two narrow procedural issues − the procedural machinery for an overruling Motion and a notification where the President does not signify his decision on a measure passed by Parliament.

sections.label: 25-Member majority for closure
sections.summary: The Committee reported that the 25-Member majority for closure of debate is not consistent with Article 57(1).

sentences.speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
sentences.text: On Mr Pritam Singh's other issue about removing the 25-Member majority for closure of debate, I would just like to reiterate what the Committee has reported, that this requirement for a 25-Member majority is not consistent with Article 57(1) which provides that all questions proposed for a discussion in Parliament shall be determined by a majority of the votes of the Members present and voting.

sections.label: No intention to close debates
sections.summary: The Government has no present intention to invoke the procedure to close debates, and the quorum Standing Order stands.

sentences.speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
sentences.text: The Government has no present intention to invoke that procedure to close debates.

sentences.speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
sentences.text: In any case, the Standing Order on quorum still stands and that is fixed at 25% of the total Members in the House.

sections.label: Risks of sitting continuously
sections.summary: Sitting in the House day in and day out risks running out of meaningful things to say and neglecting work outside Parliament.

sentences.speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
sentences.text: If we sit in the House day in and day out, not only will we run out of meaningful things to say, we risk neglecting our work outside Parliament.

sentences.speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
sentences.text: In the US, a Senator has actually gone to the extent of reading bedtime stories in the Senate to filibuster proceedings.

sections.label: Parliament as contest of hearts
sections.summary: The House is an arena for a contest of hearts and minds, and Members share a duty to maintain Parliament's standing as an effective and efficient institution.

sentences.speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
sentences.text: After all, the very purpose of this House is to be an arena for a contest of hearts and minds.

sentences.speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
sentences.text: But as Members of Parliament, we also share a common duty to maintain the standing of Parliament as an effective and efficient institution.

sentences.speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
sentences.text: I hope that this is something that all Members will support fully.

sections.label: Deferring Bill for public petition
sections.summary: The speaker asks the Leader of the House to confirm that deferring a Bill or Motion for an important public petition is conceivable in future.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
sentences.text: My exhortation was actually to the House as a whole, that there may be a real scenario in the future where it may be more in the public interest actually to defer a Bill or Motion because an important public petition has been presented.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
sentences.text: I would like the Leader of the House's confirmation that it is conceivable in the future that this might have to happen.

sections.label: Sequencing Question Time as art
sections.summary: Sequencing Question Time is more art than science because the length of Members' speeches often cannot be determined beforehand.

sentences.speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
sentences.text: Unfortunately, I think when it comes to sequencing Question Time, it is probably more art than science primarily because, very often, we are unable to determine beforehand the length of speeches that Members will make.
